title: Modern atomic theory
summary: Orbitals, quantum numbers and how electrons are arranged in an atom.
cards.0.p: According to de Broglie, an electron also behaves like a wave. According to Heisenberg, an electron's position and speed cannot both be known exactly at the same time. So Schrödinger gave the electron an orbital instead of a path. An orbital is a region where the electron is likely to be found.
cards.0.key: An orbital drawing is the surface inside which the electron is found 90% of the time.
cards.0.once.soru: Can we measure both the position and the speed of an electron exactly at the same time?
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.neden: According to Heisenberg, the more exactly the position is known, the less certain the speed becomes. So an electron is given a region of probability, not a path.
cards.0.once.secenekler.1.neden: The problem is not the instruments but nature itself. A better instrument does not remove this uncertainty.
cards.0.once.secenekler.2.yazi: Only when it is at rest
cards.0.once.secenekler.2.neden: An electron is never at rest. Its position and speed never become certain together.
cards.1.p: Four quantum numbers give each electron's address. n gives the shell, ℓ the subshell and its shape, mℓ the orientation, and ms the spin. The first three describe the orbital, and the fourth describes the electron.
cards.1.etk.soru: Match each quantum number with what it tells you.
cards.1.once.soru: A home address is given by country, city, street and house number. How many numbers give the address of an electron in an atom?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: n gives the shell, ℓ the subshell, mℓ the orbital and ms the spin. So four quantum numbers are needed.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: A single number only gives the shell. Many electrons share the same shell.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: Two numbers find the subshell, but they do not say which orbital or which electron.
cards.2.h: n and ℓ: shell and subshell
cards.2.p: n takes values such as 1, 2, 3 and gives the shell. ℓ takes values from 0 up to n − 1. The values 0, 1, 2 and 3 of ℓ stand for the s, p, d and f subshells.
cards.2.svg#18: ℓ is at most n − 1: there is no 1p, 2d or 3f subshell
cards.2.key: Shell n has n² orbitals and holds at most 2n² electrons. These numbers are 2, 8, 18 and 32.
cards.3.p: mℓ takes the whole-number values from −ℓ to +ℓ, and each value stands for one orbital. So s has 1 orbital, p has 3, d has 5 and f has 7. ms is +½ (↑) or −½ (↓).
cards.3.key: The number of orbitals in a subshell is 2ℓ + 1.
cards.3.once.soru: In the p subshell (ℓ = 1) the values of mℓ are −1, 0 and +1. How many orbitals does p have?
cards.3.once.secenekler.0.neden: Each value of mℓ stands for one orbital. There are three values, so there are three p orbitals.
cards.3.once.secenekler.1.neden: A single orbital is found in the s subshell. In p, mℓ takes three values.
cards.3.once.secenekler.2.neden: 6 is the most electrons the p subshell can hold. The number of orbitals is 3.
cards.4.h: Shapes of s, p, d and f orbitals
cards.4.p: The s orbital is spherical. The p orbitals are dumbbell-shaped, and there are three of them. Most d orbitals look like a four-leaf clover. The s subshell holds 2 electrons, p holds 6, d holds 10 and f holds 14.
cards.4.key: All s orbitals are spherical, and the sphere gets bigger as n grows. So 1s < 2s < 3s.
cards.4.once.soru: Which shape is an orbital whose probability is the same in every direction at the same distance from the nucleus?
cards.4.once.secenekler.0.neden: The shape that is the same in every direction is a sphere, which is the s orbital.
cards.4.once.secenekler.1.neden: A dumbbell-shaped p orbital stretches along one axis. So it is not the same in every direction.
cards.4.once.secenekler.2.neden: The lobes of clover-shaped d orbitals point in certain directions.
cards.5.h: Filling order: the n + ℓ rule
cards.5.p: By the Aufbau principle, an electron goes into the lowest-energy orbital first. The sum n + ℓ sets the order, and the one with the smaller sum fills first. For example, 4s has a sum of 4 and 3d has a sum of 5, so 4s fills first.
cards.5.svg#26: if n + ℓ is equal, smaller n first
cards.5.etk.soru: Tap the subshells in the order electrons fill them.
cards.6.p: By the Pauli principle, no two electrons in an atom can have all four quantum numbers the same. Electrons in the same orbital have opposite spins. So an orbital holds at most 2 electrons (↑↓).
cards.6.svg#12: One orbital: at most 2 electrons, opposite spins
cards.6.once.soru: Two electrons go into one orbital. What must their spins be?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: Two electrons in the same orbital share n, ℓ and mℓ. All four numbers cannot be the same, so their spins are opposite (↑↓).
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: Then all four quantum numbers would be the same. That is not allowed.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: It does matter, because two electrons with the same spin cannot share an orbital.
cards.7.p: By Hund's rule, electrons go into orbitals of equal energy one at a time first, all with the same spin. Pairing starts only when every orbital is half full. For example, nitrogen's 2p³ electrons are placed ↑ ↑ ↑.
cards.7.key: Think of seats on a bus. Everyone first takes an empty double seat, and only then do others sit next to them.
cards.8.p: To write an electron configuration, list the subshells in filling order, with a superscript for the number of electrons. For example, Cl is written 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵. The lowest-energy configuration is the ground state. When an electron has moved up to a higher orbital, the atom is in an excited state.
cards.8.key: In an excited state the number of electrons does not change. One electron just moves to a higher orbital.
cards.8.once.soru: Chlorine (17) has the configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵. What does the sum of the superscripts give?
cards.8.once.secenekler.0.neden: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 5 = 17, the number of electrons in neutral chlorine. Each superscript is the number of electrons in that subshell.
cards.8.once.secenekler.1.neden: The number of shells is the largest value of n, which is 3 here.
cards.9.p: A long configuration is shortened by writing the symbol of the previous noble gas in square brackets. For example, Na is written [Ne] 3s¹ and Fe [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶. The electrons outside the brackets decide the chemical behavior.
cards.9.once.soru: Sodium (11) has the configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹. Its first 10 electrons match neon's (10). How is it written in short?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: The square brackets stand for neon's 10 electrons in place of 1s² 2s² 2p⁶. What is left is 3s¹.
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: Argon has 18 electrons, but sodium has only 11.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: Helium has 2 electrons. Then 2s² 2p⁶ would be missing.
cards.10.p: By the rule, Cr should be 4s² 3d⁴ and Cu 4s² 3d⁹. In reality they are [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵ and [Ar] 4s¹ 3d¹⁰. This is because a half-full or full d subshell is more stable.
cards.10.svg#39: d⁵ half full, d¹⁰ full: more stable
cards.10.key: The configurations s¹, s², p³, p⁶, d⁵ and d¹⁰ are spherically symmetric, meaning half full or full. These are more stable.
cards.11.p: In an anion, the added electron goes into the next empty place, so Cl⁻ is [Ne] 3s² 3p⁶. In a cation, electrons leave first from the shell with the largest n. For example, Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶, because 4s empties first.
cards.11.svg#26: In a cation the outermost shell (largest n) empties first
cards.11.key: The last electron in is not the first one out. 4s fills first and also empties first when the atom forms an ion.
cards.12.h: From configuration to the periodic table
cards.12.p: Elements whose configuration ends in s or p are in the A groups, and the group number is the total of the s and p electrons in the outer shell. For elements whose configuration ends in d, the total of the s and d electrons gives the B group.
cards.12.svg#6: ends in s or p: A group · ends in d: B group
cards.12.etk.soru: Match each configuration with the element's place in the periodic table.
cards.12.key: The largest n gives the period. For example, Mn is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁵, so it is in period 4, group 7B.
cards.13.p: A particle with unpaired electrons is attracted by a magnet, and it is called paramagnetic. If all its electrons are paired, it is not attracted but very weakly repelled, and it is called diamagnetic. N (2p³) is paramagnetic, and Ne (2p⁶) is diamagnetic.
cards.13.etk.soru: Put each particle in the right group based on its orbital diagram.
cards.13.etk.ogeler.6.2: In 3d⁵ all five electrons are single: ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑.
cards.13.etk.ogeler.7.2: 4s² and 3d¹⁰ are full. There are no unpaired electrons.
cards.13.once.soru: Nitrogen's three 2p electrons are spread out ↑ ↑ ↑. What happens if you bring nitrogen atoms near a strong magnet?
cards.13.once.secenekler.0.neden: A particle with unpaired electrons is attracted by a magnet. This is called paramagnetic.
cards.13.once.secenekler.1.neden: Unpaired electrons interact with a magnet.
cards.13.once.secenekler.2.neden: Weak repulsion is seen in particles whose electrons are all paired.
cards.14.p:
• An orbital is a region of probability, not a path.
• n gives the shell, ℓ the subshell, mℓ the orientation and ms the spin.
• The subshell with the smaller n + ℓ fills first. An orbital holds at most 2 electrons, and electrons first go in one at a time.
• The ground state is the lowest-energy configuration. Cr and Cu do not follow the rule.
quiz.0.q: Put each configuration in the right group.
quiz.0.e: In the ground state, electrons follow the filling order. In an excited state the number of electrons is the same, but one electron has moved up to a higher orbital. There is no 2d subshell, because ℓ can be at most n − 1. 1s³ breaks the Pauli principle.
quiz.1.q: Put these subshells in filling order using the n + ℓ rule.
quiz.1.e: The n + ℓ values are 3 for 3s, 4 for 3p, 4 for 4s, 5 for 3d, 5 for 4p and 5 for 5s. When the sums are equal, the one with smaller n fills first. So 3p comes before 4s, 3d before 4p, and 4p before 5s.
quiz.2.q: How many orbitals are there in total in the n = 3 shell?
quiz.2.e: For n = 3, ℓ can be 0, 1 or 2, so there are 3s, 3p and 3d subshells. Their orbitals add up to 1 + 3 + 5 = 9.
quiz.3.q: What is the ground-state configuration of the Cr³⁺ ion of Cr (Z = 24)?
quiz.3.e: Cr is [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵. In the cation, first the 1 electron in 4s (largest n) leaves, then 2 electrons from 3d. The result is [Ar] 3d³, with 21 electrons left.
quiz.3.y.1: The electron in 4s leaves before those in 3d. In the Cr³⁺ ion, 4s is empty.
quiz.3.y.2: Electrons leave 4s first. Also, Cr is 4s¹ 3d⁵, not 4s² 3d⁴.
quiz.3.y.3: A cation forms by giving up electrons, not adding them. 24 − 3 = 21 electrons should be left.
A:ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Give electrons an address, fill orbitals and make an ion.
A:adimlar.0.metin: Subshells are also shown by numbers: s is 0, p is 1, d is 2 and f is 3. Iron's last electrons are in 3d. Set the n and ℓ values for an electron in 3d.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.ipucu: In the d subshell ℓ = 2. For ℓ to be 2, n must be at least 3.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.tamam: n = 3 and ℓ = 2, so this subshell is 3d. m<sub>ℓ</sub> takes five values from −2 to +2, so there are five d orbitals. The fourth number, m<sub>s</sub>, is +½ or −½.
A:adimlar.1.metin: In argon the 3p subshell is full. Add electrons and stop at the element where the first electron enters 3d.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.ipucu: Where did the last electrons of K and Ca go? Stop when the first arrow appears in the 3d boxes.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: This element is scandium (21), and its configuration is [Ar] 4s² 3d¹. 4s has n + ℓ = 4 and 3d has 5, so 4s filled first. That is why the 3rd shell stopped at 8 electrons in K and Ca.
A:adimlar.2.metin: Place nitrogen's three 2p electrons in the three 2p orbitals of equal energy. If two electrons go into one box, their spins are opposite (Pauli). Build the arrangement that follows Hund's rule.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.ipucu: Electrons do not pair while there is an empty orbital. First one electron goes into each box.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.tamam: The electrons went in ↑ ↑ ↑, one at a time first and with the same spin. Nitrogen has 3 unpaired electrons. In oxygen (2p⁴) the fourth electron pairs up.
A:adimlar.3.baslik: Two elements that break the rule
A:adimlar.3.metin: Chromium breaks the rule, because one 4s electron moves to 3d. Use the switch to go to copper and look at the two candidate configurations.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: What is copper's (29) actual ground-state configuration?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: This is what the filling order predicts. But the atom is more stable when 3d is full.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: One 4s electron moves to 3d, making a full 3d¹⁰. Like the half-full 3d⁵ in chromium, this is more stable.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: 4p has higher energy than 3d. An electron does not move to 4p before 3d is full.
A:adimlar.4.metin: Iron is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶. The last electrons to go in were in 3d. So which ones leave first when an ion forms? Give up electrons and make the Fe²⁺ ion.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.ipucu: For Fe²⁺ you must give up two electrons.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.tamam: The Fe²⁺ ion is [Ar] 3d⁶, not [Ar] 4s² 3d⁴. In a cation, electrons leave first from the shell with the largest n, which is 4s. Give up one more electron and you get the half-full Fe³⁺ ion, [Ar] 3d⁵.
A:adimlar.5.baslik: Find the element from its configuration
A:adimlar.5.metin: An element's ground-state configuration is given below. Count the electrons and find where the element sits.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: Which element is this, and where is it in the periodic table?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: There are 16 electrons, so Z = 16. The largest n is 3, and the outer shell has 6 electrons in 3s² 3p⁴. So the element is in period 3, group 6A.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The group is right, but oxygen has 8 electrons (1s² 2s² 2p⁴). Here the largest n is 3.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The group number comes from the total of the s and p electrons in the outer shell, not just the p electrons. 2 + 4 = 6.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.3.neden: Argon's 3p subshell is full (3p⁶, 18 electrons). Here 3p has 4 electrons.
A:kapanis.0: An orbital is a region where the electron is likely to be found. It is not an exact path like Bohr's orbit.
A:kapanis.1: n gives the shell, and ℓ gives the s, p, d and f subshells. ℓ can be at most n − 1. In 3d, n = 3 and ℓ = 2, and there are five orbitals.
A:kapanis.2: Electrons go first into the orbital with the smaller n + ℓ, so 4s fills before 3d. By the Pauli principle, an orbital holds at most two electrons with opposite spins.
A:kapanis.3: By Hund's rule, electrons go into orbitals of equal energy one at a time first, with the same spin. Nitrogen's electrons are placed ↑ ↑ ↑.
A:kapanis.4: Cr [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵ and Cu [Ar] 4s¹ 3d¹⁰ break the rule. When a cation forms, 4s empties first, so Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶.
